narrative.text: The foreword by the WHO Director-General argues that technology has always driven health gains and lists digital advances from point-of-care testing to artificial intelligence. It stresses that countries should be guided by evidence rather than new gadgets and presents this as WHO's first guideline on digital interventions.

Thanks the WHO coordinators, the Norwegian Institute of Public Health methods team and the many WHO staff and regional advisers. It names guideline development group members, systematic review authors, external reviewers, observers and funders.
A list of abbreviations used in the digital health guideline.

The executive summary explains the terms digital health, eHealth and mHealth and the 2018 World Health Assembly resolution, and warns against rolling out digital tools without evidence. It uses an adapted Tanahashi framework to link digital interventions to health system gaps in accountability, supply, demand, quality and affordability. It sets out the guideline's aims and stresses that digital tools do not replace functioning health systems. The end shows how ten recommendations, from birth and death notification to telemedicine, decision support and training content, fit across the health system.

The background defines digital health, eHealth and mHealth and notes over a thousand recorded digital health deployments since 2008. It recalls the 2018 Assembly resolution and warns that many tools are rolled out without evidence of benefit, so their effects must be evaluated.

Explains how digital health relates to universal health coverage using an adapted Tanahashi framework. It describes performance layers for accountability, supply, demand, quality and affordability where gaps reduce coverage. It ends with a figure showing how digital interventions, applications and health content make up digital health implementations.

States that the guideline responds to the 2018 Assembly resolution by evaluating evidence on digital health interventions, including benefits, harms, feasibility and equity. It stresses that digital tools complement but do not replace core health system components, and lists the interventions reviewed, from birth notification to training content for health workers.

Names ministry of health decision-makers and public health practitioners as the main audience, with development partners also served, and notes that recommended interventions can be used on any digital device.

Explains that WHO has not yet issued guidelines on which digital interventions have evidence behind them, though some clinical guidelines include digital tools. It describes related WHO resources such as the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, the Global Observatory for eHealth, the classification of digital interventions, the Digital Health Atlas and Be He@lthy, Be Mobile.

Explains that the maturity of the enabling and ICT environments strongly influences how relevant and effective the recommended digital interventions will be, defining both terms. It advises assessing ecosystem readiness and, where it is weak, strengthening the health system and the enabling environment before implementation.

Stresses that digital health interventions should fit into a wider digital health architecture so that systems work together rather than as isolated duplicates. It points stakeholders to complementary guidance, such as the WHO/ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit and the ITU Digital Health Platform Handbook, and lists related networks and communities of practice.

Describes the "living guidelines" approach, under which the guideline covers a prioritised subset of mobile-accessible digital health interventions and will add further interventions and health areas as evidence emerges. It gives targeted client communication for noncommunicable diseases as an example of a planned extension.
Outlines how the guideline was developed under the WHO handbook for guideline development, through two online surveys and three in-person meetings held between 2016 and 2018.

Describes how priority questions were identified, starting from a 2016 advisory meeting that used the WHO Classification of digital health interventions and framed questions in PICO format. It explains how the questions were refined through virtual and scoping meetings and online surveys that rated outcomes, with over 300 respondents across WHO regions.

Lists the digital health interventions prioritised for evidence review, including birth and death notification, stock management, client-to-provider and provider-to-provider telemedicine, targeted client communication, decision support, digital tracking and digital training of health workers. A table defines each intervention with its synonyms and descriptors. The section also sets out the health areas and outcomes considered for each intervention. It notes that the reviews required a mobile component but that the recommendations may also apply to non-mobile devices such as desktop computers.

Explains that no restrictions were placed on delivery channels and describes the two main types of evidence used: effectiveness studies such as randomised trials and controlled before-and-after studies, and qualitative studies on acceptability, feasibility and implementation. It notes that evidence on resource use and cost-effectiveness came from what the reviews found. An overarching analysis drew together qualitative reviews, an overview of systematic reviews and mixed-methods analyses.

Describes how risk of bias in effectiveness studies was assessed using Cochrane methods and how qualitative studies were appraised with an adapted Critical Appraisal Skills Programme tool. It also mentions the WEIRD tool for programme data and the use of GRADE for effectiveness evidence. Confidence in qualitative findings was graded with GRADE-CERQual as high, moderate, low or very low by consensus.

Sets out the roles of the groups that guided guideline development, including the WHO steering group drawn from many departments, the technical team of methodologists, the guideline development group and the external review group. It describes how members were chosen for geographical and gender balance. It also explains how declarations of interest were collected and managed, with biographies posted on the WHO website.

Explains how evidence profiles were consolidated into evidence-to-decision frameworks covering effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility, resource use, and gender, equity and rights. Judgements on these criteria guided the guideline development group's decisions.

Describes how the guideline development group reviewed evidence-to-decision frameworks at a June 2018 meeting and reached recommendations through discussion and voting. It defines the recommendation categories, including recommended, not recommended, recommended only in specific contexts and recommended only in the context of rigorous research. It also explains how members with declared conflicts of interest could join discussions but not vote on the related questions.
Explains how the draft guideline was prepared after the final meeting, reviewed by the guideline group and external peer reviewers, revised, and returned to members for approval.
Explains that recommendations appear in the executive summary, with evidence summaries in Chapter 3, and that relevant existing WHO recommendations are quoted exactly with added remarks where needed.

Introduces the chapter presenting ten evidence-based recommendations on the prioritised digital health interventions, listing what is given for each: background, evidence, recommendation with justification and implementation considerations. It refers to annexes and web supplements for evidence gaps and evidence-to-decision frameworks.

Summarises cross-cutting qualitative findings on how acceptable and feasible health workers find digital interventions. Factors that may increase acceptability include the chance for health workers to take on new and more senior tasks, while concerns include extra workload and the cost of using personal phones. Feasibility issues such as connectivity, power, training and device costs are also discussed. The section ends with findings on clients, including privacy worries among people with stigmatised conditions.

Covers digital birth and death notification, linking it to the global plan to strengthen civil registration and vital statistics systems and the spread of mobile phones in resource-limited settings. It summarises evidence on effectiveness, acceptability and feasibility, including community sensitivities around stillbirths and maternal deaths and the need for local staffing. WHO recommends digital birth notification only where notifications provide individual-level data and the health or civil registration system can respond. Implementation considerations include data validation, health worker reporting targets and whether registration systems can absorb more notifications.

Covers digital stock notification and commodity management, explaining why stock-outs persist, especially in rural areas, and how mobile tools such as text messaging and dashboards can help track supplies. WHO recommends this intervention only where supply chain systems can respond promptly and appropriately to notifications, despite limited evidence on effectiveness. Implementation considerations are listed against the WHO/ITU eHealth strategy toolkit framework.

Covers client-to-provider telemedicine as a way to overcome geographic barriers and uneven distribution of health workers, defining telemedicine and its forms. It summarises evidence on effects, acceptability and feasibility, including access issues for people with hearing impairments or low digital literacy. WHO recommends it only as a complement to face-to-face care in settings able to monitor safety, privacy, traceability, accountability and security for patients, followed by implementation considerations.

Covers provider-to-provider telemedicine, which links less skilled health workers with specialists for diagnosis, remote monitoring and case management, either in real time or by store-and-forward exchange. It summarises the evidence on effects, acceptability and feasibility. WHO recommends it where safety, privacy, traceability, accountability and security for patients can be monitored, including procedures for consent, data protection and checking health worker credentials, followed by implementation considerations.

Covers the recommendation on targeted client communication in WHO's guideline on digital interventions for health system strengthening, although the block's title refers to child and adolescent health. It defines the intervention as sending health information, reminders and test result notifications to specific people based on their health status or demographics, through channels such as text messages and voice calls. It reviews the evidence on effectiveness and the considerations behind the recommendation. It ends with implementation advice, including negotiating with mobile network operators over communication costs, before the next section on effective coverage.

Covers the guideline section on decision support tools for health workers, starting from the definition of quality of care and the reasons it is often poor in low- and middle-income countries. It reviews how digital decision support aims to improve health workers' adherence to recommended practice and the evidence and considerations behind the recommendation. It notes that such tools are often integrated with digital health records and points to the section on combining them with digital tracking.

Covers the guideline section on digital tracking of clients' health status and services combined with decision support and targeted client communication. It explains how digital registers and electronic records reduce the clerical burden of paper systems and support follow-up and continuity of care. It sets out the evidence and conditions for the recommendation, including concerns about privacy and data security. It closes by urging that local policies on digital identity be considered so that programmes do no harm.

Covers the guideline section on digital provision of training and educational content to health workers, describing eLearning and mobile learning delivered by text messages, apps, games and other channels, especially in remote or low-resource settings. It reviews the evidence and considerations for the recommendation. Implementation advice includes letting health workers store content for later and offering modular material they can tailor to their needs.

Opens the chapter on implementation considerations, noting that digital health shares the general health system challenges of governance, training, infrastructure and supplies, so the wider enabling environment is critical.

Explains how the guideline's separate recommendations on digital interventions link together across the health system, serving managers, clients and health workers through stock notification, telemedicine, targeted communication, decision support and mobile learning. A figure maps each recommendation to health system needs such as availability, accessibility and quality.

Sets out the components on which digital health implementations depend: accurate health content, the digital intervention itself, the software and communication channels that deliver it, and the ICT and enabling environment. A figure shows how these components combine.

Presents overarching considerations for implementing digital health, stressing fit with local needs, users and the ICT and enabling environment, and referring to the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit for assessing readiness. A table describes components of the enabling environment such as leadership and governance, strategy and investment, legislation, infrastructure and workforce. It closes with principles for digital development, including designing with users, building for scale and sustainability, using open standards, and addressing privacy and security.
Introduces the chapter on future research, which covers cross-cutting evidence gaps on effectiveness, cost, gender, equity and rights, plus specific research questions for each intervention.

Describes overarching research gaps found during guideline development, where evidence was of low or very low certainty or absent, often owing to poor reporting, small studies and limited settings. It calls for future research on health system process improvements, resource use and equity effects. It also raises questions on implementing interventions faithfully at scale and suggests frameworks such as RE-AIM to structure implementation research.

Lists the guideline group's suggestions for designing future evaluations of digital health interventions, such as alternatives to randomized trials for complex system-level interventions and attention to intermediate outcomes. It also calls for common metrics and tools for assessing effectiveness and cost-effectiveness.
A section heading for the chapter on disseminating and updating the guideline, with no further text.

Describes how WHO will disseminate the digital health guideline in full and condensed versions through regional offices, global digital health networks, regional consultations and webinars. It also mentions an implementation guide that will provide a stepwise process for fitting recommended interventions to local needs and contexts.

Explains that the guideline will be treated as a living guideline, with new evidence reviewed as it emerges, and that the first update will add targeted client communication for noncommunicable diseases in version 1.1. It notes the need for continuous scanning of the rapidly changing digital health field.

A glossary of terms used in the digital health guideline, defining words such as client, eHealth, mHealth, enabling environment and interoperability. It explains that client, individual and patient may be used interchangeably.
The reference list for the digital health guideline, citing mainly WHO publications and resolutions on eHealth and mHealth, systematic reviews and other sources on digital interventions.
A heading page marking the start of the annexes.

Annex 1 reproduces WHO's Classification of digital health interventions, listing interventions for clients, health workers, health system managers and data services, alongside a list of health system challenges such as information gaps, poor quality, workforce shortages, low demand and loss to follow-up. It also cites the source classification document. The block ends with the heading for Annex 2.

Annex 2 sets out the guideline's priority questions in PICO format, covering populations, digital interventions accessible via mobile devices, comparators and outcomes. Interventions include birth and death notification, stock notification, telemedicine, targeted client communication, decision support, digital tracking and mobile learning. Outcomes include data use, efficiency, service use, health outcomes, acceptability and cost-effectiveness, with the health domains covered by the systematic reviews.

Lists the contributors to the WHO guideline on digital health interventions, including guideline development group members and co-chairs with their affiliations, external reviewers and WHO staff from headquarters and regional offices.

A table summarising declarations of interest by guideline development group members, with the action taken for each, such as exclusion from voting on recommendations linked to reviews they led. Most members declared no interests.

Presents evidence maps showing the certainty of effectiveness evidence for each digital health intervention, mostly low or very low, across outcomes for clients and health workers. Separate tables cover client interventions such as targeted client communication, health worker interventions and health system interventions. A further table lists research gaps with illustrative research questions, including cross-cutting gaps on gender, equity and rights. The section ends with WHO's address and the ISBN.

The front matter of the 2019 WHO guideline on digital interventions for health system strengthening, with the copyright, licence and ISBN page and the table of contents. The contents run through the introduction, methods and recommendations to the web supplements on evidence-to-decision frameworks and GRADE tables.
